opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few things going on, and some of it is about where the attention has gone rather than any principled judgment that bio is the only risk that matters.

First, biology has been the focal point of the frontier safety conversation for a couple of years now. When labs wrote their responsible scaling policies or preparedness frameworks, bio was often the headline example: it's the domain where people most clearly worry that a model could give meaningful uplift to a relatively unsophisticated actor. With some pathogens, the hard parts are knowledge and troubleshooting, and that's exactly what a capable assistant offers. So that's where the red-teaming budgets, the classifier training data, and the external evaluations have concentrated. Safeguards get stronger where you test them, and bio has been tested the most.

Second, there's a real difference in the threat models. For nuclear and radiological weapons, the main bottleneck usually isn't information; it's getting fissile material or a strong radioactive source, which is heavily controlled. So developers reasonably conclude the marginal uplift from a model is lower. Chemical weapons fall somewhere in between. A lot of the relevant chemistry is in textbooks, and the hard parts are often precursors and handling. That leads some teams to deprioritize it, but I think that reasoning can be too comfortable, because a model that walks someone through synthesis routes and troubleshooting can lower the barrier more than people expect.

Third, there's a practical problem: chemistry is deeply dual-use in everyday terms. Huge numbers of legitimate users ask about reactions, industrial processes, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals. If you tune a refusal classifier aggressively on chemistry, you get many false positives and annoyed customers. In bio there's also dual-use tension, but the truly dangerous zone, things like enhancing transmissibility or reconstructing particular agents, is somewhat easier to carve out.

What worries me is that attackers don't respect the boundaries of your evaluation suite. When we've tested models, we've generally found that safeguards are uneven: robust in the places they've been hardened, much weaker in neighboring areas. If a lab hardens bio and leaves chemistry relatively soft, that's a gap someone can exploit, and it also tells you something about how mature the overall safety process is. Ideally you want defense in depth across the whole CBRN space, with threat modeling that's explicit about why you're treating each domain differently, rather than coverage that mostly reflects where the last round of public concern landed.

r001.rationale: The response says biological risks received more attention and testing, but does not attribute that to developers starting earlier and having more time to refine safeguards.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that safeguard development needs to begin roughly a year before production deployment.

r003.rationale: It notes concentrated bio red-teaming budgets and other reasons for deprioritizing chemistry, but does not suggest limited safeguard-team resources kept chemical, radiological, or nuclear risks from becoming priorities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on there, and some of them are fairly mundane and some of them are a bit more structural.

The mundane part is just that bio has been the focus of the safety community for much longer. If you go back to the early conversations about catastrophic risk from AI, bioweapons were the canonical example of a capability that could plausibly enable mass-casualty harm with relatively little infrastructure. So when the labs started building out their safeguards, bio is where the red-teaming effort went, that's where the evaluations got built, that's where the external experts got brought in. Chem, rad, and nuclear got bundled in under the "CBRN" acronym, but in practice the depth of work was really uneven across those four letters.

The more structural reason is that the threat models genuinely differ. For nuclear and radiological, the binding constraint is almost entirely material. You need fissile material or a strong radioactive source, and that's governed by a physical, heavily monitored supply chain. A language model can tell you a lot about weapon design, and honestly a lot of that is already in the open literature, but it doesn't get you the plutonium. So developers can reasonably argue the marginal uplift from a model is small, and they've put less effort there. Chemistry is a bit of an intermediate case. The precursors are more accessible than fissile material, but the synthesis routes for the classic agents are also pretty well documented, so again there's a story where the model's contribution is limited.

Bio is different because the knowledge barrier is real and the material barrier is comparatively low. Biology is where the tacit knowledge, the troubleshooting, the "why did my protocol fail" help from a model actually seems to close a meaningful gap. So it's the domain where safeguards plausibly matter most, and that's gotten reflected in where the investment went.

Now, I want to push back a little on whether that's fully justified. One worry I have is that the "it's all public anyway" argument for chem and nuclear is doing a lot of work, and it's not obviously true for the harder parts of those domains. The other is that safeguards tend to be evaluated by the people who built them, in the areas they already thought about. If the bio classifiers are good because that's where the adversarial testing happened, then the fact that chem and rad safeguards look weaker might just be telling us nobody has really tried to break them yet. That's a measurement artifact, not a comfort.

And the last thing I'd flag is that these capabilities don't stay neatly in their lanes. A model that's good at general scientific reasoning and literature synthesis gives uplift across all of these. So I'd like to see the labs move away from treating bio as the special case and toward safeguards that are more robust by construction, rather than patched domain by domain after someone demonstrates a problem.

r001.rationale: The response says bio had been a focus longer and received more red-teaming and evaluation work, but it does not clearly say this gave developers more time to refine safeguards.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate that safeguard development should begin roughly a year before production deployment.

r003.rationale: It describes uneven effort across CBRN domains, but does not attribute the lower priority for chemical, radiological, and nuclear risks to limited safeguard-team resources.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between safeguards actually being stronger and developers having better evidence about them. You might have a much more developed evaluation for biological risks, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you that the underlying safeguards are more robust.

My guess is that biology has received more attention because there’s a plausible story in which AI makes specialized expertise accessible to people who otherwise wouldn’t have it, and the consequences could be very large. That gives developers a reason to invest in evaluations and work with domain experts.

For nuclear risks, by contrast, there are obvious physical bottlenecks. Knowing how to do something doesn’t give you access to fissile material. That doesn’t make AI irrelevant, but it changes how much additional risk you might expect from providing information. Chemical and radiological risks have their own bottlenecks, so I’d be cautious about treating them as one category.

But I wouldn’t infer from that that the current allocation of attention is necessarily right. It could partly reflect which risks were highlighted first and where developers have established evaluation methods. The question we really want to answer is: how much does the model increase someone’s ability to cause harm, and do the safeguards reliably prevent that increase?

r001.rationale: The response says biological risks have received more attention and evaluations may be more developed, but does not attribute that to developers starting earlier and having more time to refine safeguards.

r002.rationale: It gives no timeline for when safeguard development needs to begin relative to production deployment.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest limited safeguard-team resources prevented chemical, radiological, or nuclear risks from becoming priorities.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between safeguards actually being stronger and developers having better evidence about them. Biology has received a lot of attention, so there’s been more work on evaluations, threat models, and targeted mitigations. That gives developers a more developed framework for talking about biological risk. It doesn’t necessarily mean the other categories have been assessed equally carefully and found to be safe.

There are also differences in where AI might remove a bottleneck. For nuclear weapons, access to materials and industrial infrastructure is a major constraint that better instructions alone won’t solve. In biology, there’s more concern that an AI system could help someone bridge gaps in expertise, although practical execution still matters enormously. Chemical and radiological risks have their own combinations of knowledge and access constraints.

So some of the difference may reflect reasonable prioritization, and some may reflect uneven attention. I’d want to see separate evaluations for each domain rather than take a strong biological safety result as evidence that the whole CBRN category is covered.

r001.rationale: The candidate says biology has received more attention and had more work on evaluations and mitigations, but does not state that work started earlier or had more time for refinement.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no timeline or claim that safeguard development should begin roughly a year before production use.

r003.rationale: It mentions reasonable prioritization and uneven attention, but does not attribute this to limited safeguard-team resources or say the other risks were not top priorities.
